newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Booker profits slump after charges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Booker profits slump after charges.

text.p: Food distributor Booker Plc posted a sharp drop in its 1996 profits on Tuesday, hit by an exceptional charge of 89 million pounds ($143.9 million), but steady sales growth figures and a confident trading outlook helped push the shares higher.
Booker posted 1996 pretax profits, excluding exceptional items, of 101.9 million pounds up from 100.6 million. Sales rose five percent to 4.443 billion.
But exceptional charges came to 88.9 million, due mainly to the integration of Nurdin and Peacock acquired in November and the reorganisation of Booker Foodservice.
Booker shares were up 5-1/2p at 341p in early trade.
In an interview, chief executive Charles Bowen said slow profits growth was forecast for 1997 but shareholders could expect a substantial return in 1998.

"There is a lot to do this year, we are working very hard but we are trying to stop people getting too excited too early. In 1997 we will show a small amount of growth but in 1998 shareholders can expect a significant return," Bowen said.
Booker has seen like-for-like sales growth of five to six percent in its cash and carry business since its year ended December 28, said Bowen.
About two thirds of the company's overall profits come from cash and carry. The like-for-like growth is in line with figures released by Britain's major supermarkets.

He said the stock market is forecasting pretax profits for Booker of 105 million pounds for 1997, after the de-consolidation of its Portugese business, a number which the company would not argue too much with.
"The overall message about this year is there are no surprises -- we are on track and the year has started as we expected it to."
The acquisition of N&P in November created a cash and carry wholesale business with combined sales of 4.0 billion pounds and purchasing strength comparable to that of major supermarket groups.
Bowen said Booker still had considerable costs to get out of integrating N&P, representing 10 million pounds in the first year and more than twice that by 1999.
As a result of the acquisition Booker is benefitting from an increased purchasing power and savings in distribution, he said.
Bowen said the company's target to reduce debt by at least 100 million by the end of 1998 from its current 420 million remains on track.
On the poultry side Booker suffered from steep rises in U.S. feed costs, which also affected the level of orders from its major customers.
The company's food service division, especially Holroyd Meek, was affected by a very tough contract catering distribution market and severe pressure on margins.
Trading profit from food service fell to 8.6 million in 1996 from 13.3 million stg. Booker expects this business will continue to be difficult in 1997.
The company's largest division, food wholesaling, posted trading profits of 73.0 million pounds in 1996, up from 57.7 million previously. ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
